XVIII.1.title: Three good men of the Yin
XVIII.1.reflection: Under the last cruel king of the Shang, the Viscount of Wei left, the Viscount of Ji became a slave, and Bigan remonstrated and was killed. Confucius says the Yin had three humane men. Three different responses to a tyrant, all called ren.
XVIII.1.question: Faced with a wrong you cannot stop, would you leave, endure or speak?

XVIII.2.title: Dismissed three times
XVIII.2.reflection: Liuxia Hui, a judge, was dismissed three times. Why not leave the state? If I serve men straightly, where would I not be dismissed three times? If I serve them crookedly, why leave my parents' land? Integrity will cost the same everywhere.
XVIII.2.question: What would your integrity cost you anywhere you went?

XVIII.3.title: Between Ji and Meng
XVIII.3.reflection: Duke Jing of Qi debates how to treat Confucius: not as the head of the Ji, but between the Ji and the Meng. Then: I am old, I cannot use him. Confucius leaves. Book XVIII records the departures of his wandering years.
XVIII.3.question: When have you been offered a place and not a purpose?

XVIII.4.title: The dancing girls
XVIII.4.reflection: Qi sends female musicians to Lu; Ji Huanzi accepts them and holds no court for three days. Confucius leaves. Tradition dates his departure from Lu, at about fifty-five, to this episode. The chapter blames the man who stopped governing, not the women who were sent.
XVIII.4.question: What distraction has made you neglect your work?

XVIII.5.title: The madman of Chu
XVIII.5.reflection: Jieyu, the madman of Chu, passes singing: phoenix, phoenix, how your virtue has declined; the past cannot be helped, the future can still be saved; stop, stop, those who govern now are in danger. Confucius gets down to speak with him, but he hurries away. The hermits address Confucius as a phoenix in the wrong age.
XVIII.5.question: Who has warned you to give up, and were they wrong?

XVIII.6.title: Asking the way to the ford
XVIII.6.reflection: Two recluses are ploughing; Zilu asks one where the ford is. Is your master Kong Qiu? Then he knows the ford. The other: the whole world is a flood; who can change it? Better follow men who leave the world than one who leaves particular men. Confucius sighs: I cannot live with birds and beasts; if not with people, with whom? If the world had the Way, I would not try to change it. The most direct answer to the hermits in the book.
XVIII.6.question: Whom do you stay with, though it would be easier to withdraw?

XVIII.7.title: The old man with the basket
XVIII.7.reflection: Falling behind, Zilu meets an old man carrying a weeding basket. Your four limbs do not toil, you cannot tell the five grains apart: who is your master? Yet he takes Zilu in, kills a chicken, makes millet and introduces his sons. When Zilu returns, the man is gone, and Zilu speaks for the school: not to serve is not right; one cannot keep order between old and young and abandon the duty between ruler and minister. The junzi serves to do what is right, knowing the Way may not prevail.
XVIII.7.question: When has someone who disagreed with you treated you with great kindness?

XVIII.8.title: The recluses
XVIII.8.reflection: Confucius names seven who withdrew from the world and judges them: some kept their will and body unsullied, some bent but spoke and acted rightly, some lived hidden and spoke freely. As for me, I differ: I have no fixed for or against. The last line repeats IV.10.
XVIII.8.question: Do you have positions you must take no matter what?

XVIII.9.title: The musicians scatter
XVIII.9.reflection: The grand music master went to Qi, the masters of the second, third and fourth meals to Chu, Cai and Qin, the drummer across the river, the hand-drummer to the Han, the chime player to an island in the sea. A list of departures that says, without comment, that the court music of Lu fell apart.
XVIII.9.question: What has scattered that once gathered in one place?

XVIII.10.title: The Duke of Zhou to his son
XVIII.10.reflection: The Duke of Zhou tells his son, ruler of Lu: do not neglect your kin, do not leave great ministers resentful of being unused, do not dismiss old servants without grave cause, do not expect one person to do everything. Advice from the founder of Lu, the man Confucius dreamed of in VII.5.
XVIII.10.question: From whom do you expect everything?

XVIII.11.title: Eight officers of Zhou
XVIII.11.reflection: Zhou had eight officers, named in four pairs. Tradition says they were twins, born to one mother. It is a list remembered for its own sake, closing a book of departures with an image of plenty.
XVIII.11.question: Whom would you name if asked for the good people of your time?
